'''Paul Hagenmuller''' (August 3, 1921 – January 7, 2017) was a French chemist. Hagenmuller founded the Laboratoire de Chimie du Solide (Solid-State Chemistry Laboratory) of the [[French National Centre for Scientific Research]] (CNRS) and he served as its Director until 1985. He is considered "one of the founders of [[solid-state chemistry]]."<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Pouchard|first=Michel|date=2017-06-12|title=Paul Hagenmuller (1921–2017)|journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition|language=en|volume=56|issue=25|pages=7032|doi=10.1002/anie.201703788|pmid=28523724 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Hagenmuller was born in 1921 in [[Alsace]], [[France]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Teissier |first=Pierre |date=2008 |title=Paul Hagenmuller. Itinéraire de l'enfant terrible de la chimie du solide française. |url=https://halshs.archives-ouvertes.fr/halshs-01078854 |journal=L'Actualité Chimique |language=fr |issue=319 |pages=France}}</ref> After studying in [[Strasbourg]] and [[Clermont-Ferrand]], during [[World War II|WW2]], Hagenmuller was imprisoned in the [[Buchenwald concentration camp|Buchenwald]] and [[Mittelbau-Dora concentration camp|Mittelbau-Dora]] concentration camps. During those years, he was involved in sabotaging German missiles.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Paul Hagenmuller {{!}} In memoriam {{!}} Membres {{!}} Nous connaître|url=https://www.academie-sciences.fr/en/In-memoriam/paul-hagenmuller.html|access-date=2021-12-15|website=www.academie-sciences.fr}}</ref> In 1950 he received his PhD from [[Sorbonne University]]. Subsequently, he spent two years teaching as a lecturer (''[[maître de conférences]]'') in Vietnam. He returned to France in 1956 and was appointed Professor of Inorganic Chemistry at the [[University of Rennes]], working on "nonstoichiometry in vanadium and tungsten bronzes, two-dimensional oxyhalogenides, borides, and silicides, magnetic spinels". In 1961 he started working at the [[University of Bordeaux]].<ref name=":0" />

Hagenmuller was noted for instigating cooperation between French researchers and researchers from the Soviet Union and Germany, his years in the concentration camps greatly affected his character.<ref name=":1"/> He also collaborated with noted scientists such as  [[John B. Goodenough|John Goodenough]], [[Jacques Friedel]] and [[Nevill Francis Mott]] on insulator-to-metal transitions of [[vanadium oxide]]s. In the 1970s, he started working with [[Neil Bartlett (chemist)|Neil Bartlett]] on metal [[fluoride]]s. His most noted research discovery was the synthesis of {{Chem|La|Cu|O|3}} and {{Chem|La|Sr|Cu|O|4}}, which would later become important superconductor materials.<ref name=":0" /> His work on [[Sodium-ion battery|sodium-ion batteries]] received great interest years after it was published.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=El Aichouchi|first1=Adil|last2=Gorry|first2=Philippe|date=June 2018|title=Paul Hagenmuller's contribution to solid state chemistry: A scientometric analysis|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022459618300501|journal=Journal of Solid State Chemistry|language=en|volume=262|pages=156–163|doi=10.1016/j.jssc.2018.02.003|bibcode=2018JSSCh.262..156E |s2cid=102618815 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In 2018 Hagenmuller remained the 4th most cited author from the [[Journal of Solid State Chemistry]].<ref name=":2"/>

* [[Gay-Lussac Humboldt Prize]] (1982)
* [[Prix de la Fondation de la Maison de la Chimie]] (1986)
